## Every hop in your trace names its heuristic {.smaller}

**Bottom line:** this afternoon's trace follows the ransom to the first service. At every hop you write which heuristic took you there, what could make it wrong, and how sure you are. This lesson teaches the heuristics and how they fail.

| For every hop, write | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Where the money went | `T4`, output 1, to a fresh `bc1q...` address |
| The heuristic that says so | Change: fresh address, same script type as the inputs |
| What could make it wrong | Both outputs are fresh and of the same type |
| How sure, on the course scale | Moderate |

: {tbl-colwidths="[40,60]"}

Two Bitcoin heuristics, **co-spending** and **change**, are the base of Bitcoin tracing [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013; @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022].

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide opens lesson ② by tying it to the afternoon's lab product, the annotated trace. It matters here because the trace's graded point is that each hop names its heuristic. Emphasize that the four columns are the habit: destination, heuristic, failure, confidence.

**Key Points**
- The trace runs from the ransom payment to the first service.
- Every hop records the heuristic, what could break it, and a confidence on the course scale (High, Moderate, Low; never a percentage).
- Co-spending and change come from Meiklejohn et al. (2013); Kappos et al. (2022) describe the co-spend heuristic as the one now widely used for tracing.
- New glossary terms this lesson: cluster, co-spend heuristic, change output, super-cluster, peel chain, peel, payment batching, backward trace.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read the bottom line.
2. Walk the four rows using the example hop.
3. Say: by the end of the lesson you can fill every row for any hop.

**Sources**
- @meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013
- @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022

:::

## Co-spending links inputs, unless it's a CoinJoin {.smaller}

**Bottom line:** addresses spent together as inputs to one transaction most likely belong to one owner. That holds by habit, not by rule, and a CoinJoin breaks it on purpose.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **The heuristic:** all inputs to one transaction are controlled by the same user [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013].
- **Why it works:** each input needs its own key's signature, so multi-input transactions "necessarily reveal that their inputs were owned by the same owner" [@nakamoto_bitcoinpeertopeerelectronic_2008].
- **Why it fails:** a CoinJoin puts several people's inputs into one transaction [@gmaxwell_coinjoinbitcoinprivacy_2013]; spotting one is day 3. A 2022 test set counts every cluster holding a CoinJoin as merging owners: 60 of its 120 [@kappos_howpeelmillion_2022].
- **How sure:** co-spending alone is **Moderate**.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{dot}
//| fig-width: 4.5
//| fig-height: 3.4
digraph CoSpend {
  rankdir=TB;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="#f8fafc", color="#cbd5e1", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=13];
  edge [color="#64748b", arrowsize=0.7, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11];

  A1 [label="A1", fillcolor="#fef3c7", color="#f59e0b"];
  A2 [label="A2", fillcolor="#fef3c7", color="#f59e0b"];
  T1 [label="Ordinary spend:\none wallet", fillcolor="#dcfce7", color="#22c55e"];
  X [label="Alice", fillcolor="#fef3c7", color="#f59e0b"];
  Y [label="Bob", fillcolor="#e0f2fe", color="#38bdf8"];
  Z [label="Carol", fillcolor="#fce7f3", color="#ec4899"];
  T2 [label="CoinJoin:\nthree owners", fillcolor="#fee2e2", color="#ef4444"];

  A1 -> T1; A2 -> T1;
  X -> T2; Y -> T2; Z -> T2;
  {rank=same; A1; A2; X; Y; Z;}
  {rank=same; T1; T2;}
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide teaches the co-spend (common-input-ownership) heuristic and its main failure. It matters here because co-spending is how a trace grows from one address to a cluster, and the lab asks for a confidence on every co-spend link. Emphasize that the heuristic rests on how wallets usually behave; a CoinJoin is built to defeat it.

**Key Points**
- Meiklejohn et al.'s Heuristic 1: the inputs of one transaction are controlled by one user.
- Nakamoto's paper names the leak: multi-input transactions reveal a common owner.
- A CoinJoin combines several users' inputs; applying co-spending to it merges strangers.
- Kappos et al.'s ground-truth set held 120 clusters; the 60 false positives each contained one or more CoinJoins.
- Co-spending alone rates Moderate: one strong line, with a known false positive.
- Define cluster briefly: a set of addresses the analyst believes one entity controls.

**Walkthrough**
1. Left: A1 and A2 signed by one wallet. One owner, most likely.
2. Right: three people sign one transaction. The same shape, three owners.
3. Ask: from the inputs alone, can you always tell the two apart? (No; day 3 shows the clues.)

**Sources**
- @meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013
- @nakamoto_bitcoinpeertopeerelectronic_2008
- @gmaxwell_coinjoinbitcoinprivacy_2013
- @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022

:::

## One false link merges two actors into one {.smaller}

**Bottom line:** clusters grow by chaining: if A and B co-spend, and B and C co-spend, all three join. So one wrong link joins two whole clusters.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
- **Super-cluster:** false change links merged Mt. Gox, Instawallet, BitPay and Silk Road into one cluster of 1.6 million keys [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013].
- **A huge cluster is usually a service:** 20 ransomware addresses sat in clusters averaging 2.9 million addresses, all exchanges, wallets, mixers or markets [@kappos_howpeelmillion_2022].
- **So:** write down the heuristic behind every link, so a reader can find and cut a bad one.
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
```{dot}
//| fig-width: 4
//| fig-height: 3.8
digraph Merge {
  rankdir=TB;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="#f8fafc", color="#cbd5e1", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=13];
  edge [color="#64748b", arrowsize=0.7, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11, dir=none];

  subgraph cluster_x {
    label="Actor X"; fontname="Helvetica"; fontsize=12; color="#f59e0b"; style="rounded";
    A [label="A"]; B [label="B"]; C [label="C"];
  }
  subgraph cluster_y {
    label="Actor Y"; fontname="Helvetica"; fontsize=12; color="#38bdf8"; style="rounded";
    D [label="D"]; E [label="E"];
  }
  A -> B [label="co-spend"];
  B -> C [label="co-spend"];
  D -> E [label="co-spend"];
  C -> D [label="one false\nchange link", color="#ef4444", fontcolor="#b91c1c", style=dashed];
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide shows why clustering errors are expensive: links are transitive, so one false link merges two entities. It matters here because the lab's trace and day 3's memo both depend on clusters a reader can audit. Emphasize recording the heuristic behind each link.

**Key Points**
- Clustering chains links; a single false link merges two clusters.
- Meiklejohn et al. warn that falsely linking even a few change addresses can collapse the graph into super-clusters, and they hit one of 1.6 million public keys.
- Kappos et al.: of their ransomware addresses, 20 sat in clusters averaging 2.9 million addresses, all tagged as exchanges, hosted wallets, mixers or darknet markets; size suggests a custodial service, not one person.
- Kappos et al. add that nested services (services operating through accounts at an exchange) appear as the exchange under co-spending alone.
- Define super-cluster briefly: a cluster that has wrongly merged many unrelated entities.

**Walkthrough**
1. A, B and C join by co-spending: actor X. D and E: actor Y.
2. One false change link from C to D.
3. Now X and Y look like one actor, and every conclusion about "them" mixes two people.

**Sources**
- @meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013
- @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022

:::

## Change is a guess from several weak clues {.smaller}

**Bottom line:** the change output returns money to the payer and moves the trace on. Every clue below is a wallet habit, so none is proof [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013].

| Clue | Points to change when | Fails when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fresh address | Only this output's address is new [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013] | Both are new |
| Script type | Its type matches the inputs' [@kappos_howpeelmillion_2022] | Payee's wallet is the same type |
| Un-round amount | 0.2937 beside a round 1.00 [@kappos_howpeelmillion_2022] | Both are un-round |
| Output position | The wallet always puts change first, or last [@kappos_howpeelmillion_2022] | The wallet varies it |
| Next hop alike | Later spent with the same transaction settings [@kappos_howpeelmillion_2022] | Both are spent alike |

: {tbl-colwidths="[20,52,28]"}

**How sure:** one clue alone is **Low**; several agreeing are **Moderate**, because all come from the same transaction. On a rough reuse test, 13% of Meiklejohn's first change labels looked wrong [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013].

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide turns 02-BF's change clues into a method: list the clues, say when each points to change and when it fails. It matters here because change detection decides where every hop of the trace goes next. Emphasize that agreeing clues raise confidence only to Moderate: they are one kind of evidence, the transaction's own shape.

**Key Points**
- Meiklejohn et al.'s Heuristic 2: a one-time change address is controlled by the inputs' owner. They note it rests on an idiom of use, not on the protocol, so it is less robust than co-spending.
- Kappos et al. use address type, output index and the transaction features of the next hop ("the same transaction settings": version, SegWit, locktime, replaceability); they note earlier change heuristics relied on address freshness and output values, including a rule that the change value is significant to at least the fourth decimal place (Ermilov et al.).
- Meiklejohn et al.'s first attempt flagged over 4 million change addresses; to estimate false positives they counted labeled addresses later reused, 13%. They judged many of those (such as Satoshi Dice payouts) not truly false, so the figure is rough. Refinements cut it, but the super-cluster still formed.
- Course scale: amount or behavior alone is Low; weaker lines that agree are Moderate; independent means a different kind of evidence, so more clues from the same transaction do not make High.
- Define change output briefly: the output that returns the unspent remainder of the inputs to the payer.

**Walkthrough**
1. Take 02-BF's example: Alice pays Bob 1.00 and A3, new, gets 0.29.
2. Run down the table: fresh, same type, un-round. Three clues agree.
3. Rate it: Moderate. Ask: what would raise it to High? (A different kind of evidence, such as off-chain information; day 3.)

**Sources**
- @meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013
- @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022

:::

## Two outputs aren't always payment and change {.smaller}

**Bottom line:** when the clues don't tell the outputs apart, don't pick one. Write "change undetermined" and keep both as leads.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **Two payees, no change:** mining pools and gambling sites often pay two people at once [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013].
- **Look-alike outputs:** in the Bitcoin Fog case, both outputs of one hop were fresh, of one type and spent alike; no change rule could follow it [@kappos_howpeelmillion_2022].
- **Wallets that break the habit:** some let the user choose or reuse the change address [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013].
- **What to do:** follow both outputs, or trace backward from where the money ended.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{dot}
//| fig-width: 4.5
//| fig-height: 3.6
digraph Undetermined {
  rankdir=TB;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="#f8fafc", color="#cbd5e1", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=13];
  edge [color="#64748b", arrowsize=0.7, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11];

  I [label="Input: 1.2441 BTC", fillcolor="#fef3c7", color="#f59e0b"];
  T [label="One transaction\nfee 0.0002 BTC", fillcolor="#e0f2fe", color="#38bdf8"];
  O1 [label="0.5317 BTC\nfresh, bc1q"];
  O2 [label="0.7122 BTC\nfresh, bc1q"];
  Q [label="Which is change?\nUndetermined", shape=note, fillcolor="#fee2e2", color="#ef4444"];

  I -> T; T -> O1; T -> O2;
  {rank=same; O1; O2;}
  O1 -> Q [style=dashed, arrowhead=none];
  O2 -> Q [style=dashed, arrowhead=none];
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide teaches when change detection should stop: the two outputs look alike, or there is no change at all. It matters here because a forced change call is the false link of the previous slide. Emphasize that "undetermined" is a correct answer in the trace.

**Key Points**
- Meiklejohn et al. note that payments to two different users are frequent (mining pool payouts, bets on gambling sites), so a two-output transaction need not have change.
- Kappos et al.'s Bitcoin Fog trace stalled forward after one hop: both outputs had the same address features, were spent in transactions with the same features, and were both fresh.
- Meiklejohn et al. found that wallets letting users specify change addresses, and change addresses used twice, produced false change labels; they excluded those cases.
- Recording "change undetermined" and keeping both outputs as candidates is better than a confident wrong hop.

**Walkthrough**
1. One input, two outputs, both fresh, both `bc1q`, neither round.
2. Run the table from the last slide: no clue separates them.
3. Write: change undetermined; candidates 0.5317 and 0.7122.

**Sources**
- @meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013
- @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022

:::

## A peel chain: a small peel, the rest rolls on {.smaller}

**Bottom line:** a peel chain starts with a large amount. Each hop pays a small amount (the **peel**) to one address and sends the rest to a fresh change address, which does it again, for hundreds or thousands of hops [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013].

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
- **Ordinary users and services make them:** exchange withdrawals and mining-pool payouts run as peel chains [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013].
- Services run scripts, so their chains are long and regular, which makes them easier to follow [@kappos_howpeelmillion_2022].
- **Thieves use them too:** stolen coins were gathered into one address, then peeled; some thieves peeled, re-gathered and peeled again [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013].
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{dot}
//| fig-width: 5.5
//| fig-height: 3.6
digraph Peel {
  rankdir=LR;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="#f8fafc", color="#cbd5e1", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=12];
  edge [color="#64748b", arrowsize=0.7, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11];

  S [label="Start\n20.000", fillcolor="#fef3c7", color="#f59e0b"];
  C1 [label="Change\n19.249", fillcolor="#dcfce7", color="#22c55e"];
  C2 [label="Change\n18.048", fillcolor="#dcfce7", color="#22c55e"];
  C3 [label="Change\n17.647", fillcolor="#dcfce7", color="#22c55e"];
  M [label="...", shape=plaintext, style=""];
  P1 [label="Peel 0.750"];
  P2 [label="Peel 1.200"];
  P3 [label="Peel 0.400"];

  S -> C1 -> C2 -> C3 -> M;
  S -> P1; C1 -> P2; C2 -> P3;
  {rank=same; S; P1;}
  {rank=same; C1; P2;}
  {rank=same; C2; P3;}
}
```

Each hop also pays a 0.001 BTC fee.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide defines the peel chain, the most common pattern students will follow in the lab. It matters here because a peel chain is a run of change calls, so each hop inherits the change slide's clues and failures. Emphasize that peel chains are ordinary: services make them all day, so the pattern alone says nothing about crime.

**Key Points**
- Meiklejohn et al. define the peeling chain: a large starting amount, a small peel to one address per hop, the remainder to a one-time change address, repeated potentially for hundreds or thousands of hops; leftovers may be aggregated and peeled again.
- They observed the pattern in withdrawals from banks and exchanges and in mining-pool payouts.
- Kappos et al.: peel chains are fundamental to UTXO coins (outputs cannot be partly spent), and big services' scripted payments create long, patterned chains that are easier to follow.
- Meiklejohn et al.'s theft cases: aggregation then peeling (Betcoin), and peel-and-aggregate repeated (Bitfloor).
- Define peel briefly: the small output at each hop, paid away from the chain.

**Walkthrough**
1. Start: 20.000 BTC.
2. Hop 1: 0.750 peeled; 0.001 fee; 19.249 rolls on as change.
3. Hop 2: 1.200 peeled; 18.048 rolls on. Hop 3: 0.400 peeled; 17.647 rolls on.
4. Ask: which output carries the chain forward? (The large change.)

**Sources**
- @meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013
- @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022

:::

## Follow the remainder; the peels are your leads {.smaller}

**Bottom line:** at each hop, the change output takes you to the next hop and the other output is the peel: the money's real recipient. Record every peel; the first one that lands at a service is where your trace ends [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013].

- **Betcoin, 2012:** 3,171 BTC stolen in April 2012 sat unmoved until March 2013. It was then gathered into one address and peeled. After 10 hops a peel went to the Bitcoin-24 exchange; 10 hops later, one went to Mt. Gox. In all, 374.49 BTC reached known exchanges straight off the chain [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013].
- **Ransomware, 2022:** 96% of the peels from ransomware peel chains went to one-time addresses. That fits exchange deposit addresses, but the authors say it "does not clearly imply this" [@kappos_howpeelmillion_2022].
- **For each peel, record:** amount, address, hop number and what that address does next.
- **Naming the service** that owns a deposit address is attribution: day 3.

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide teaches the tracing method for a peel chain: follow the change, collect the peels. It matters here because the lab's trace ends at the first service, and that is almost always a peel landing in a deposit address. Emphasize that a one-time recipient address suggests a service but does not prove it.

**Key Points**
- Meiklejohn et al.'s method: at each hop, follow the change address to the next transaction; the other output is the meaningful recipient (the peel).
- Betcoin: hacked 11 April 2012, 3,171 BTC stolen in four installments; aggregated 15 March 2013 and peeled; peels to Bitcoin-24 after 10 hops and to Mt. Gox 10 hops later; 374.49 BTC to known exchanges directly off the main chain.
- Kappos et al. collected 91,493 counterparty addresses from ransomware peel chains; 96% were one-time addresses, consistent with exchange deposit addresses, which the authors stress is not proof.
- Attribution, linking a deposit address to a named service, is day 3.

**Walkthrough**
1. Return to the previous slide's chain: the green boxes are the path, the white boxes are the leads.
2. Tell the Betcoin story: wait, gather, peel, and peels reaching exchanges within 20 hops.
3. Ask: the 96% figure, is it evidence that the recipients are exchanges? (Weak and consistent, not proof: Low.)

**Sources**
- @meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013
- @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022

:::

## Batched payouts look busy but aren't a peel {.smaller}

**Bottom line:** services, "mainly exchanges", often pay many customers in one transaction, a **batch** [@bitcoinoptech_paymentbatching_2021]. A batch most often means a service paying out, so your trace has likely reached one: **Low** until attribution (day 3).

| | Peel-chain hop | Batched payout |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Outputs | Two: one peel, one change [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013] | Many: one per customer, often plus change [@bitcoinoptech_paymentbatching_2021] |
| Inputs | The previous hop's change [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013] | The service's own, ideally just one [@bitcoinoptech_paymentbatching_2021] |
| What co-spending links | The inputs to the payer | The inputs to the service, never the customers to each other |
| What you write | Follow the change; record the peel | Likely a service (Low); your subject's output is the lead |

: {tbl-colwidths="[22,36,42]"}

- **Why only Low:** any wallet can pay many outputs at once, and thieves split funds too [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013]; the shape alone is behavior.
- **Watch for:** exchanges also pay withdrawals as peel chains [@meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013].

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide sets an exchange's batched payouts beside a peel chain (adversarial review P1). It matters here because a batch's many outputs can look like a suspect fanning money out, and misreading it sends the trace into dozens of unrelated customers. Emphasize the reading: a batch most often means the money is inside a service, and the output that matters is the one your subject received; but the shape alone is behavior, so it rates Low until attribution.

**Key Points**
- Optech: payment batching includes multiple payments in one transaction; it is used mainly by exchanges; an unbatched payment typically has one input and two outputs (receiver and change), while a batch adds an output per receiver, ideally from a single input.
- Optech lists reduced privacy as a cost: recipients of one batch can assume a common sender.
- Co-spending links inputs only, so a batch says nothing about whether its recipients know each other.
- Optech says services batch, not that only services do: any wallet can pay several outputs, and Meiklejohn et al.'s theft cases include thieves splitting funds. Shape alone is Low.
- Meiklejohn et al. saw peel chains in exchange withdrawals too; both shapes can be a service paying customers.
- Define payment batching briefly: paying many recipients in one transaction to save fees.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read the two columns row by row.
2. Ask: your subject's address is one of 40 outputs of a batch from an exchange. What do you write? (Funds likely came from a service, Low until attribution; if so, the subject withdrew from it and the other 39 are other customers.)

**Sources**
- @bitcoinoptech_paymentbatching_2021
- @meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013

:::

## When forward fails, trace backward {.smaller}

**Bottom line:** a trace can run either way. When change is undetermined going forward, start from where the money ended and work back. As described by Kappos et al. in 2022 [@kappos_howpeelmillion_2022]:

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **The question:** did a 2011 Mt. Gox withdrawal fund a deposit into the Bitcoin Fog mixer? Roman Sterlingov had a Mt. Gox account in his real name.
- **Forward:** every change rule stopped after one hop, at two look-alike outputs.
- **Backward:** from the deposit, the trace reached the withdrawal in seven hops.
- **Backward can mislead:** it gives more false positives than forward; in 2011 every transaction looked alike.
- **Record** the direction you traced and where forward stopped.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{dot}
//| fig-width: 4.5
//| fig-height: 3.8
digraph Backward {
  rankdir=TB;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="#f8fafc", color="#cbd5e1", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=13];
  edge [color="#64748b", arrowsize=0.7, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11];

  W [label="tx1: Mt. Gox withdrawal\n(he held an account there)", fillcolor="#fef3c7", color="#f59e0b"];
  H [label="tx2: two look-alike outputs\nforward stops", fillcolor="#fee2e2", color="#ef4444"];
  M [label="intermediate hops", shape=plaintext, style=""];
  D [label="tx3: Bitcoin Fog deposit", fillcolor="#e0f2fe", color="#38bdf8"];

  W -> H [label="forward"];
  W -> M [dir=back, label="backward:\n7 hops in all", color="#22c55e", fontcolor="#15803d"];
  M -> D [dir=back, color="#22c55e"];
  {rank=same; H; M;}
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide teaches the backward trace through a real case. It matters here because the lab's ransom trace may stall at an undetermined hop, and working back from a known endpoint is the way through. Emphasize the method, not the case's legal outcome, which is outside the course.

**Key Points**
- Kappos et al., section 7.3.1: an IRS special agent's affidavit linked a 2011 deposit to the Bitcoin Fog cluster with a withdrawal from the Mt. Gox cluster where Sterlingov had an account in his real name.
- The receiving and sending clusters were different, so co-spending alone could not link them; the IRS affidavit said the withdrawal funded the deposit.
- Forward following failed after one hop: tx2's two outputs had the same address features, were spent in transactions with the same features, and were both fresh.
- Following backward from the deposit reached the withdrawal after seven hops; the authors note the agent likely did this by hand.
- They warn that backward following is more prone to false positives than forward: in 2011 all transactions had the same features, so it could run back indefinitely without noticing a change of owner. Here three deposit paths led to the same origin, which made them more sure.
- Describe the case as the 2022 paper does; its later court history is not taught here.
- Define backward trace briefly: following funds from where they ended to where they came from.

**Walkthrough**
1. Top: the withdrawal. Forward, the trace stops at tx2.
2. Bottom: the deposit. Backward, hop by hop, the trace reaches tx1 in seven hops.
3. Ask: in your trace, which endpoints do you know? (The ransom address, and possibly a service's deposit.)

**Sources**
- @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022

:::

## Same-transaction clues never reach High alone {.smaller}

**Bottom line:** confidence rises with independent evidence, not more clues: clues from the same transactions stop at Moderate.

| Hop rests on | Confidence | Why, on the course scale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Change from one clue, such as a round amount | **Low** | Amount or behavior alone |
| Co-spending, no sign of a CoinJoin | **Moderate** | One strong line; CoinJoin is a known false positive |
| Several change clues that agree | **Moderate** | Weaker lines, all from the same transaction |
| A long peel chain with a steady pattern | **Moderate** | One kind of evidence: the pattern |
| Any of these, plus another kind of evidence (day 3) | **High** | Independent lines agree; no known failure applies |

: {tbl-colwidths="[42,16,42]"}

Investigators "should not rely on" these heuristics "as definitive evidence": a careful actor defeats them [@kappos_howpeelmillion_2022].

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide applies the course confidence scale to the heuristics taught so far. It matters here because every hop in the lab trace carries a confidence, and the common mistake is to count clues instead of kinds of evidence. Emphasize the definition: independent means a different kind of evidence, not a second heuristic over the same transactions.

**Key Points**
- Low: timing, amount or behavior alone, or one unverified label.
- Moderate: one strong line, or weaker lines that agree, with a known false positive possible.
- High: two or more independent lines agree and no known failure applies; on-chain heuristics alone do not get there.
- Kappos et al. warn that randomizing transaction and address features defeats their heuristics and that investigators should not rely on them as definitive evidence; they add that all clustering heuristics share these limits but still work because many entities do not evade them.
- Never give a percentage.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read each row and its reason.
2. Ask: three change clues agree; is that High? (No: Moderate. Same transaction, same kind of evidence.)

**Sources**
- @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022

:::

## A worked trace: four steps, four judgments {.smaller}

**Bottom line:** your lab product looks like this: one row per judgment, with its heuristic, its failure and its confidence. (Invented data.)

| Step | What you see | Heuristic | Could be wrong if | Confidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Ransom R1 and R2 spent together in `T1` | Co-spend: one wallet | `T1` is a CoinJoin | Moderate |
| 2 | `T1` pays 0.5000 to P, 2.4137 to C1 | Change is C1: fresh, same type, un-round | C1 is the payment | Moderate |
| 3 | C1 peels 0.1 to 0.6 over hops `T2` to `T6` | Peel chain: follow the change | A peel was the change | Moderate |
| 4 | `T6`'s peel to D; D's cluster: 2 million addresses | Huge cluster: likely a service | It is not a service | Low |

: {tbl-colwidths="[7,30,26,22,15]"}

Stop at step 4: the money has reached what looks like a service. Naming it, and raising that Low, is day 3.

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide models the annotated trace the lab asks for, on invented data. It matters here because students see a finished product before they build one. Emphasize that every row names a heuristic and a failure, and that the trace stops at the first service.

**Key Points**
- Step 1: co-spending of two ransom addresses in one transaction; Moderate because a CoinJoin would break it.
- Step 2: the same transaction's outputs; three change clues agree; Moderate, since they are one kind of evidence.
- Step 3: a peel chain of five transactions followed by its change; each hop inherits the change rule's failure.
- Step 4: the last peel lands in address D, later co-spent into a cluster of about 2 million addresses (service-sized, like the 2.9 million average on the false-link slide); a huge cluster is usually a service, but size alone is behavior, so Low until attribution.
- A row is one judgment, so one transaction can give two rows (steps 1 and 2) and a peel chain one row (step 3).
- The data are invented for illustration; the lab uses its own captured data.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read each row left to right: what moved, why you think so, what would make you wrong, how sure.
2. Ask: why does the trace stop at step 4? (It has reached the first service.)
3. Ask: which row would you check first if the conclusion were challenged? (The weakest: step 4.)

**Sources**
- @meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013
- @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022

:::

## Recap: every hop, a heuristic and a confidence {.smaller}

- **Co-spending** links a transaction's inputs to one owner; a CoinJoin breaks it. Alone: Moderate.
- **One false link** merges two actors; a huge cluster is usually a service.
- **Change** is a guess from weak clues; when they don't separate the outputs, write "undetermined".
- **Peel chains:** follow the change; the peels are the leads, and the first peel at a service ends the trace.
- **Batches** most often mean a service paying customers: likely a service, Low until day 3.
- **Backward** works when forward stalls; record the direction.
- **Confidence** rises with independent evidence, not with more clues.
- **This afternoon:** the annotated trace. **Day 3:** CoinJoin and mixers, attribution, and the first memo.

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide summarizes the heuristics and their failures and hands over to the lab. It matters here because the annotated trace uses every line. Emphasize the habit: heuristic, failure, confidence, for every hop.

**Key Points**
- Co-spending and its CoinJoin failure.
- False links, super-clusters and service-sized clusters.
- Change clues and the undetermined case.
- Peel chains, peels as leads, batches as likely services.
- Backward tracing.
- Confidence by kinds of evidence.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
- @meiklejohn_fistfulbitcoinscharacterizing_2013
- @kappos_howpeelmillion_2022
- @bitcoinoptech_paymentbatching_2021
- @gmaxwell_coinjoinbitcoinprivacy_2013

:::

## Recall: UTXO vs. Account Model {.smaller}

| | **Bitcoin (UTXO)** | **Ethereum (Account)** |
|---|---|---|
| **How value moves** | Outputs are created and consumed — each coin has a traceable history | Balances update in place — accounts persist and change state |
| **Tracing unit** | Individual UTXOs (discrete coin fragments) | Addresses and contract interactions |
| **Where evidence lives** | Transaction inputs and outputs | Transaction record + event logs + internal call traces |
| **Hidden value flows** | Rare — the tx record is mostly complete | Common — ERC-20 transfers and internal calls are invisible without parsing logs |
| **Primary heuristic** | Common-Input-Ownership (CIOH) | Contract interaction clustering |

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This opening comparison slide establishes that Bitcoin and Ethereum require different forensic mental models because value and evidence are recorded differently. It matters here because the rest of the lesson depends on not applying UTXO heuristics blindly to account-based systems. Emphasize that the tracing unit changes the entire investigative workflow.

**Key Points**
- Bitcoin traces discrete outputs, while Ethereum often traces persistent accounts, contract calls, and event logs.
- Analysts need to know where evidence actually lives before selecting heuristics or tools.
- Spell out UTXO as unspent transaction output and define event log as contract-emitted data that records token and application activity.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@gjorgjev_blockchainforensicsunmasking_2025; @salisu_blockchainforensicsmodern_2023

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Reminder: Bitcoin's UTXO Model

Transactions **consume** old outputs and **create** new ones. Every satoshi has a traceable ancestry.

::: {style="z-index: -1; position: relative; top: -75px; max-height: 440px; overflow: hidden;"}

```{dot}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.2
digraph UTXO {
  graph [bgcolor="transparent"];
  rankdir=LR;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="#f5f7fb", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9];
  edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=8];

  utxo_a [label="UTXO A\n0.6 BTC", fillcolor="#E6F7FF"];
  utxo_b [label="UTXO B\n0.5 BTC", fillcolor="#E6F7FF"];
  tx [label="Transaction", shape=ellipse, fillcolor="#fdd"];
  out1 [label="Output 1\n1.0 BTC\n(Payee)", fillcolor="#e8f5e9"];
  out2 [label="Output 2\n0.09 BTC\n(Change)", fillcolor="#E6F7FF"];

  utxo_a -> tx;
  utxo_b -> tx;
  tx -> out1;
  tx -> out2;
}
```

:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Implication:** If you know one input address, the Common-Input-Ownership Heuristic (CIOH) lets you cluster all co-spent inputs as the same owner. Outputs can be identified as payment vs. change using heuristics.
:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide establishes the UTXO model as the foundation for classic Bitcoin forensics heuristics. It matters here because later heuristics such as CIOH and change detection only make sense in this model. Emphasize that value moves by consuming and recreating outputs rather than mutating balances in place.

**Key Points**
- Every Bitcoin transaction consumes prior outputs and creates new ones with their own traceable histories.
- The structure makes payment and change inference possible when paired with heuristics.
- Define CIOH briefly as the common-input-ownership heuristic that assumes co-spent inputs are controlled by one entity.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@gjorgjev_blockchainforensicsunmasking_2025; @salisu_blockchainforensicsmodern_2023

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Reminder: Ethereum's Account Model

Accounts **persist**. Transactions update balances — and trigger contract code, which may move value through many more contracts in a single block.

::: {style="z-index: -1; position: relative; top: -50px; max-height: 400px; overflow: hidden;"}

```{dot}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.2
digraph Ethereum {
  graph [bgcolor="transparent"];
  rankdir=LR;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10, fillcolor="#f5f7fb"];
  edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10];

  eoa [label="EOA\n(Your Wallet)", fillcolor="#E6F7FF"];
  contract [label="Smart Contract\n(e.g., Uniswap)", fillcolor="#fff5cc"];
  token [label="Token Contract\n(e.g., USDT)", fillcolor="#e8f5e9"];
  eoa2 [label="EOA\n(Recipient)", fillcolor="#E6F7FF"];

  eoa -> contract [label="1. Call swap()"];
  contract -> token [label="2. Internal call"];
  token -> eoa2 [label="3. Transfer event (log)", style=dashed, color="#2ecc71", fontcolor="#2ecc71"];
}
```

:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Implication:** The top-level transaction may show $0 ETH transferred. All value movement is in the logs. You must parse every contract's event log to follow the money.
:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide establishes the account model as the reason Ethereum forensics often requires deeper parsing than Bitcoin. It matters here because a simple transaction view can hide most of the actual value movement. Emphasize that contracts, logs, and traces must be read together.

**Key Points**
- Ethereum accounts persist over time, and contracts can trigger many downstream actions from one top-level transaction.
- Analysts often need logs and traces because top-level ETH value fields can be misleading or zero.
- Define internal trace briefly as the record of contract-to-contract execution steps inside one transaction.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@gjorgjev_blockchainforensicsunmasking_2025; @salisu_blockchainforensicsmodern_2023

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## The Analyst's Mindset: Graph Thinking {.smaller}

Blockchain forensics is fundamentally **graph analysis**. On-chain data is represented as a network of nodes and edges to uncover patterns of activity.

-   **Nodes:** Addresses, UTXOs, or **entity clusters** — a real-world actor assumed to control all addresses in the cluster.
-   **Edges:** Transactions or value flows between nodes.

::: {style="position: relative; top: -140px; overflow: hidden; max-height: 410px; z-index: -1; padding: 0; margin: 0;"}

```{dot}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.2
digraph GraphThinking {
  graph [bgcolor="transparent"];
  rankdir=LR;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="#f5f7fb", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11];
  edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10];

  addr_a [label="Address A"];
  addr_b [label="Address B"];
  entity1 [label="Entity 1\n(Cluster: A+B)", shape=ellipse, fillcolor="#e8f5e9"];
  addr_c [label="Address C"];
  entity2 [label="Entity 2\n(Cluster: C)", shape=ellipse, fillcolor="#fdd"];

  addr_a -> entity1 [style=dashed, label="belongs to"];
  addr_b -> entity1 [style=dashed];
  addr_c -> entity2 [style=dashed, label="belongs to"];
  entity1 -> entity2 [label="Transaction", penwidth=2];
}
```


:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" style="position:relative; top:-100px;"}
By identifying recurring **motifs** — fan-outs, fan-ins, peeling chains — analysts can infer entity behavior and intent.
:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide establishes graph thinking as the core analytical mindset for blockchain forensics. It matters here because the lesson is about patterns of movement and control, not isolated transactions. Emphasize that the analyst's job is to collapse many addresses and flows into interpretable entity behavior.

**Key Points**
- Nodes can represent addresses, outputs, or clustered entities, and edges represent value movement or relationships.
- Recognizable graph motifs help analysts infer laundering strategies, service roles, or operational intent.
- Define entity cluster briefly as a set of addresses inferred to be controlled by one real-world actor or service.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@gjorgjev_blockchainforensicsunmasking_2025; @frowis_safeguardingevidentialvalue_2020

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Graph Motif: The "Fan-Out"

A **Fan-Out** occurs when a single source sends to many destinations.

```{dot}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 1.8
digraph FanOut {
  graph [bgcolor="transparent"];
  rankdir=LR;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="#f5f7fb", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11];
  input [label="Input", fillcolor="#e3f2fd", color="#0d6efd", fontcolor="#0d6efd"];
  source [label="Single Source", shape=ellipse, fillcolor="#fdd"];
  dest1 [label="Dest 1"];
  dest2 [label="Dest 2"];
  dest3 [label="Dest 3"];
  dest_n [label="...", style=dotted];

  input -> source;
  source -> dest1;
  source -> dest2;
  source -> dest3;
  source -> dest_n;
}
```

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide establishes the fan-out as a basic graph motif whose meaning depends heavily on context. It matters here because many benign and malicious behaviors can look similar at first glance. Emphasize that pattern recognition must always be paired with domain interpretation.

**Key Points**
- A fan-out means one source distributes value to many destinations.
- Exchanges, payouts, dusting attacks, and laundering steps can all produce fan-out shapes.
- Define dusting briefly as sending tiny amounts to many addresses to tag or study them.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@gjorgjev_blockchainforensicsunmasking_2025; @frowis_safeguardingevidentialvalue_2020

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Graph Motif: The "Fan-In"

A **Fan-In** consolidates many inputs into a single destination.

```{dot}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 1.8
digraph FanIn {
  graph [bgcolor="transparent"];
  rankdir=LR;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="#f5f7fb", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11];
  source1 [label="Source 1"];
  source2 [label="Source 2"];
  source_n [label="...", style=dotted];
  dest [label="Single Destination", shape=ellipse, fillcolor="#fdd"];
  output [label="Output", fillcolor="#e3f2fd", color="#0d6efd", fontcolor="#0d6efd"];

  source1 -> dest;
  source2 -> dest;
  source_n -> dest;
  dest -> output;
}
```

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide establishes the fan-in as the opposite graph motif: many sources consolidating into one destination. It matters here because consolidation often signals service infrastructure, laundering preparation, or fund aggregation. Emphasize that destination context determines whether the fan-in is routine or suspicious.

**Key Points**
- Fan-in patterns often appear when deposits are being aggregated before further movement or cash-out.
- A known destination label can turn a generic fan-in into a strong investigative lead.
- Define consolidation briefly as gathering funds from many addresses into a smaller number of controlled destinations.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@gjorgjev_blockchainforensicsunmasking_2025; @frowis_safeguardingevidentialvalue_2020

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Ethereum Forensics: Where the Evidence Hides

A top-level Ethereum transaction tells you only part of the story.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**What the transaction record shows:**

-   `from` / `to` / `value` (ETH transferred)
-   Gas used, status (success/fail)

**What it *doesn't* show:**

-   ERC-20 / ERC-721 token transfers
-   Internal calls between contracts
-   Flash loan amounts
-   DEX swap token flows
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{dot}
#| echo: false
digraph EthEvidence {
  graph [bgcolor="transparent"];
  rankdir=TB;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fillcolor="#f5f7fb"];
  edge [fontname="Helvetica"];

  tx [label="Top-Level Tx\n(value: $0 ETH)", fillcolor="#fdd"];
  logs [label="Event Logs\n(ERC-20 Transfers,\nSwap events)", fillcolor="#e8f5e9"];
  traces [label="Internal Traces\n(contract-to-contract\ncalls)", fillcolor="#fff5cc"];

  tx -> logs [label="emitted by\ncontracts"];
  tx -> traces [label="debug_trace\nTransaction"];
}
```

:::
::::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="minimal"}
A DeFi swap may show **$0 ETH** in the top-level transaction while moving **$10M in stablecoins** — all recorded only in event logs.
:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide establishes one of the biggest pitfalls in Ethereum forensics: the main transaction record often omits the economically meaningful flows. It matters here because analysts who stop at top-level fields miss most token and DeFi activity. Emphasize where the hidden evidence actually lives.

**Key Points**
- ERC-20 transfers, internal calls, and flash-loan flows often appear only in logs or traces, not the top-level `value` field.
- Ethereum investigations are incomplete without token and contract parsing.
- Define DeFi briefly as decentralized finance applications built from smart contracts.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@gjorgjev_blockchainforensicsunmasking_2025; @salisu_blockchainforensicsmodern_2023

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Following Token Flows: ERC-20 Transfers

ERC-20 tokens (USDT, USDC, WETH, etc.) are the dominant form of value in DeFi. Their transfers are **invisible in the main transaction record**.

Every ERC-20 transfer emits a log event from the token contract:

```
Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint256 value)
```

::: {style="overflow: hidden; position: relative; max-height: 300px; top: -100px;"}
```{dot}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 1.8
digraph ERC20 {
  graph [bgcolor="transparent"];
  rankdir=LR;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11, fillcolor="#f5f7fb"];
  edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10];

  eoa1 [label="EOA A\n(Sender)"];
  router [label="DEX Router\n(Contract)", fillcolor="#fff5cc"];
  token [label="USDT Contract\n(ERC-20)", fillcolor="#e8f5e9"];
  eoa2 [label="EOA B\n(Receiver)"];

  eoa1 -> router [label="Tx: swap()\nETH value: $0"];
  router -> token [label="internal: transferFrom()"];
  token -> eoa2 [label="LOG: Transfer\n$500,000 USDT", style=dashed, color="#2ecc71", fontcolor="#2ecc71"];
}
```
:::



**Forensic implication:** To trace USDT, USDC, or any token, you must query the *token contract's* event logs — not the sending transaction.

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide establishes ERC-20 transfer events as the primary evidence stream for token-denominated tracing on Ethereum. It matters here because stablecoins and wrapped assets dominate many high-value illicit flows. Emphasize that token contracts, not just user wallets, become the forensic recordkeepers.

**Key Points**
- ERC-20 token movement is recorded through emitted `Transfer` events rather than the top-level ETH value field.
- Stablecoin tracing depends on querying token contract logs directly.
- Spell out ERC as Ethereum Request for Comments and define stablecoin as a token designed to track a reference asset such as the U.S. dollar.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@gjorgjev_blockchainforensicsunmasking_2025; @salisu_blockchainforensicsmodern_2023

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Smart Contract Forensics

Three patterns every Ethereum forensics analyst must recognize:

**Proxy Contracts (EIP-1967)**
:   The address you see called on-chain is a thin shell that forwards all calls to a separate *implementation* contract. The code executing is NOT at the address you're looking at. Analysts must resolve the proxy to understand what ran.

**Flash Loans**
:   Borrowed and repaid within a single transaction — creating a distinctive trace signature of a massive inflow immediately followed by repayment. Often the first step in price manipulation exploits. The entire attack can happen in one block.

**Reentrancy**
:   The same contract is called multiple times recursively within a single transaction trace. A classic exploit pattern (The DAO, 2016) — detectable in traces but invisible at the transaction level.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
These patterns are only visible in **transaction traces** (`debug_traceTransaction`). Etherscan's UI parses some of this, but automated forensic investigation requires trace-level data from an archive node or a provider like Alchemy/Infura.
:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide establishes the contract-level patterns analysts must recognize before they can interpret complex Ethereum incidents. It matters here because proxies, flash loans, and reentrancy can radically change what a transaction means. Emphasize that smart-contract architecture shapes trace interpretation.

**Key Points**
- Proxies, flash loans, and reentrant execution all produce trace signatures that can mislead an unprepared analyst.
- Understanding contract patterns is necessary to avoid misattributing intent or execution path.
- Define proxy briefly as a contract that forwards execution to another implementation contract.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@gjorgjev_blockchainforensicsunmasking_2025; @salisu_blockchainforensicsmodern_2023

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Address Clustering {.smaller}

The foundational rule for clustering Bitcoin addresses is the **Common-Input-Ownership Heuristic (CIOH)**:
*If a transaction has multiple inputs, all inputs are controlled by the same user — because signing requires possession of all corresponding private keys.*

::: {style="position: relative; z-index: -1; top: -50px; margin: 0; max-height: 410px; padding: 0;"}


```{dot}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 0.8
digraph CIOH {
  graph [bgcolor="transparent",  nodesep=0.25, ranksep=0.4, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=8];
  rankdir=LR;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="#f5f7fb", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=8];
  edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=7];

  subgraph cluster_tx {
    label="Single Transaction";
    style=dashed;
    tx [label="Transaction", shape=ellipse, fillcolor="#fdd"];
    input1 [label="Address A (Input)"];
    input2 [label="Address B (Input)"];
    input1 -> tx;
    input2 -> tx;
  }

  subgraph cluster_entity {
    label="Analyst's Conclusion";
    style=dashed;
    entity [label="Entity 1", shape=cylinder, fillcolor="#e8f5e9"];
  }

  input1 -> entity [label="Belongs to", style=dashed];
  input2 -> entity [label="Belongs to", style=dashed];
}
```

:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
By repeatedly applying CIOH, a single known address can expand into a large cluster — providing a complete picture of an entity's activity.
:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide establishes CIOH as the foundational Bitcoin clustering heuristic, while also signaling that it is an inference rather than a law. It matters here because clustering is powerful only when its assumptions are understood. Emphasize why co-signing implies likely shared control in ordinary transactions.

**Key Points**
- Multiple inputs in one standard Bitcoin transaction often indicate one controller with all needed private keys.
- Repeated application of CIOH can grow one known address into a much larger cluster.
- Define clustering briefly as grouping multiple addresses or outputs into one likely entity.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@frowis_safeguardingevidentialvalue_2020

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Heuristic #2: Change Address Detection 

In the UTXO model, transactions often have two outputs: one to the payee, one back to the sender as **change**. Identifying the change output expands an entity's cluster.

**Heuristic Indicators:**

-   **New Address:** Change address is brand new with no prior history.
-   **Script Type Match:** Change address script (e.g., P2WPKH) matches the input addresses.
-   **No "Round" Number:** Payees receive round amounts (e.g., 0.1 BTC); change is the un-round remainder.
-   **Wallet Fingerprinting:** Some wallets use a predictable output index for change (e.g., Electrum historically placed change at output index 1).
-   **Address Reuse:** If one output has appeared in prior transactions, it is likely the known payee — making the other output the change.

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide establishes change detection as the second major heuristic for expanding Bitcoin clusters beyond explicit co-spends. It matters here because much of the sender's continued control is hidden in the change output. Emphasize that change identification is probabilistic and strongest when several indicators align.

**Key Points**
- Newness, script similarity, non-round values, and wallet patterns all help identify likely change outputs.
- No single indicator is enough on its own; investigators rely on converging signals.
- Define change output briefly as the remainder returned to the sender after paying the intended recipient.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@frowis_safeguardingevidentialvalue_2020

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Heuristic #3: Peeling Chains {.smaller}

A **peeling chain** is a sequential pattern where an entity repeatedly "peels" small amounts off to destinations while sending the bulk to a new change address.

::: {style="position: relative; z-index: -1; top: -50px; margin: 0; max-height: 410px; padding: 0;"}


```{dot}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 1.9
digraph PeelingChain {
  graph [bgcolor="transparent"];
  rankdir=LR;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="#f5f7fb", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10];
  edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10];

  c0 [label="10 BTC", fillcolor="#fdd"];
  c1 [label="9 BTC", fillcolor="#fff5cc"];
  c2 [label="8 BTC", fillcolor="#fff5cc"];
  c3 [label="...", style=dotted];

  p1 [label="1 BTC\n→ Darknet", fillcolor="#e8f5e9"];
  p2 [label="1 BTC\n→ Mixer", fillcolor="#e8f5e9"];
  p3 [label="1 BTC\n→ Exchange", fillcolor="#e8f5e9"];

  c0 -> p1;
  c0 -> c1;
  c1 -> p2;
  c1 -> c2;
  c2 -> p3;
  c2 -> c3;
}
```

:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Analogous to financial "structuring" — used to send funds to high-risk destinations in small increments. Tools like **Chainalysis Reactor** and **Elliptic Investigator** automate detection by traversing transaction graphs algorithmically.
:::


::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide establishes peeling chains as one of the most recognizable laundering motifs in UTXO systems. It matters here because they turn large balances into long, repetitive transactional trails that machines can detect well. Emphasize the repeating pattern of small outward payments and one large continuing remainder.

**Key Points**
- Peeling chains structure movement into repeated small outputs and one large rolling change output.
- The pattern is laborious for humans to follow manually but highly detectable algorithmically.
- Define structuring briefly as breaking value into smaller movements to reduce attention or risk.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@chainalysis_reports_2025; @trmlabs_trmlabsreports_2025; @frowis_safeguardingevidentialvalue_2020

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Pitfalls & Counter-Heuristics

Heuristics are educated guesses, not ground truth. Blind reliance leads to errors.

-   **CIOH Fails:** Deliberately broken by **CoinJoin** — multiple users co-sign a single transaction. Assuming common ownership here falsely merges distinct entities.
-   **False Change:** Not all two-output transactions have change. A user could simply be paying two people. Misidentifying the payee as change misdirects the investigation.
-   **Wallet Variations:** Different wallets — and versions of the same wallet — behave differently. A heuristic tuned to one wallet may fail silently on another.
-   **Exchange UTXO Consolidation:** Exchanges regularly sweep thousands of customer deposits into shared hot wallets. Applying CIOH to these sweeps falsely merges thousands of unrelated users into a single "entity" — a significant source of false positives in commercial tools.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Key Point:** Heuristic-based findings are **probabilistic leads**, not definitive proof. Always seek corroborating evidence.
:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide establishes the limits of heuristic reasoning so students do not confuse useful inference with ground truth. It matters here because false clustering can derail investigations and damage credibility. Emphasize the need for corroboration before asserting ownership or intent.

**Key Points**
- Heuristics break under adversarial design, unusual wallet behavior, and institutional consolidation patterns.
- Analysts should treat heuristic outputs as leads that need confirmation, not as courtroom-ready proof.
- Define false merge briefly as incorrectly combining unrelated users or addresses into one cluster.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@frowis_safeguardingevidentialvalue_2020; @atlam_blockchainforensicssystematic_2024

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Counter-Heuristic #1: CoinJoin

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
CIOH works because **only the owner of all private keys can create a valid multi-input transaction**. This assumption is the foundation of most Bitcoin clustering.

**CoinJoin** pools multiple users' inputs into a single transaction, deliberately breaking CIOH by severing the link between sender and receiver.

:::
::: {.column width="45%"}

```{dot}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 1.5
digraph CoinJoinTx {
  graph [bgcolor="transparent", splines=ortho, nodesep=0.15, ranksep=0.4];
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9];
  edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=8];
  A_in [label="User A", fillcolor="#E6F7FF"];
  B_in [label="User B", fillcolor="#FFF5CC"];
  C_in [label="User C", fillcolor="#E8F5E9"];
  TX [label="CoinJoin", shape=ellipse, fillcolor="#fdd"];
  subgraph cluster_outs {
    label="Anonymity Set";
    style=dashed;
    fontname="Helvetica";
    fontsize=9;
    Out1 [label="Output 1"];
    Out2 [label="Output 2"];
    Out3 [label="Output 3"];
  }
  {A_in, B_in, C_in} -> TX -> {Out1, Out2, Out3};
}
```

:::
::::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="minimal"}
**Legal Status (2024):** Operators of **Samourai Wallet** were arrested on money laundering and unlicensed money transmission charges. Wasabi Wallet subsequently shut down its CoinJoin coordinator for U.S. users. Whether non-custodial CoinJoin coordination constitutes a crime is actively litigated.
:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide establishes CoinJoin as the canonical counter-heuristic designed to break CIOH. It matters here because it shows that privacy tools often target the exact assumptions analysts rely on most. Emphasize that multi-party coordination changes the meaning of multi-input transactions.

**Key Points**
- CoinJoin intentionally makes multiple unrelated users appear inside one transaction.
- This breaks naive common-input clustering and forces investigators toward other evidence sources.
- Define anonymity set briefly as the group of possible candidates among whom one participant is hidden.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@gmaxwell_coinjoinbitcoinprivacy_2013; @frowis_safeguardingevidentialvalue_2020; @departmentofjustice_operatorscryptocurrencymixers_2025

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Obfuscation Service: Mixers & Tumblers

A **mixer** breaks the chain of custody by pooling funds and redistributing them.

```{dot}
#| echo: false
digraph Mixer {
  graph [bgcolor="transparent"];
  rankdir=LR;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica"];
  edge [fontname="Helvetica"];

  subgraph cluster_inputs {
    label="Deposits";
    style=dashed;
    UserA [label="User A\n(Illicit)", fillcolor="#fdd"];
    UserB [label="User B\n(Licit)", fillcolor="#e8f5e9"];
    UserC [label="User C\n(Licit)", fillcolor="#e8f5e9"];
  }

  Mixer [label="Mixer Pool", shape=cylinder, fillcolor="#f5f7fb", height=1.5];

  subgraph cluster_outputs {
    label="Withdrawals";
    style=dashed;
    NewA [label="New Addr A'", fillcolor="#fdd"];
    NewB [label="New Addr B'", fillcolor="#e8f5e9"];
    NewC [label="New Addr C'", fillcolor="#e8f5e9"];
  }

  UserA -> Mixer;
  UserB -> Mixer;
  UserC -> Mixer;
  Mixer -> NewA;
  Mixer -> NewB;
  Mixer -> NewC;
}
```

Mixers can be centralized services or decentralized smart contracts (e.g., **Tornado Cash**, sanctioned by OFAC in 2022 for laundering funds for North Korean state actors).

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide establishes mixers as obfuscation services that break direct fund provenance by pooling and redistributing value. It matters here because mixers are a recurring pivot in laundering investigations. Emphasize that the service obscures custody links but usually creates new infrastructure that can itself be studied.

**Key Points**
- Mixers aim to sever direct transaction history between deposit and withdrawal addresses.
- Centralized and decentralized mixers introduce different legal and operational weaknesses.
- Define tumbler briefly as a service that redistributes pooled funds to obscure original custody.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@sykes_virtualcurrenciesmoney_2019; @u.s.dept.oftreasury_ustreasurysanctions_2022; @departmentofjustice_operatorscryptocurrencymixers_2025

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Breaking Mixers: Investigative Countermeasures

Despite their obfuscation, mixers have exploitable weaknesses:

-   **Timing Analysis:** If the pool has low volume, a deposit at time *T* can be correlated with a withdrawal at *T + δ*. Many mixers use insufficient time delays.
-   **Amount Correlation:** Mixers that don't standardize output denominations leak information. A deposit of 3.47 BTC with a subsequent withdrawal of 3.44 BTC (minus fee) is a strong candidate.
-   **Graph Clustering:** The mixer's own deposit and withdrawal infrastructure can be clustered. Investigators label the mixer, then focus on post-withdrawal behavior.
-   **Operational Security Failures:** Users reuse addresses, withdraw directly to KYC exchanges, or leave OSINT trails — collapsing anonymity at the human endpoint.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
**Investigator's Principle:** You rarely break the mixer cryptographically. The chain of custody almost always fails at the **human endpoints**, not the protocol. 
:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide establishes that mixers are usually broken operationally, not cryptographically. It matters here because investigators need to know where to focus effort after the trail enters a pool. Emphasize timing, amount, clustering, and user mistakes as the main attack surfaces.

**Key Points**
- Low-volume pools, imperfect denominations, and direct withdrawals to KYC services all weaken mixer anonymity.
- Post-withdrawal behavior often reveals more than the pool mechanics themselves.
- Define denomination standardization briefly as forcing withdrawals into fixed amounts to reduce amount-based correlation.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@frowis_safeguardingevidentialvalue_2020; @sykes_virtualcurrenciesmoney_2019; @atlam_blockchainforensicssystematic_2024; @l35_privacy_pools_docs_2026; @boneh_zeroknowledgeproofs_2020

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## The Next Generation: Privacy Pools

In response to Tornado Cash sanctions, **Privacy Pools** attempts to balance privacy with compliance.

-   **Like a mixer:** Uses **zero-knowledge proofs** (ZKPs) to break the deposit-withdrawal link. A ZKP proves a statement is true without revealing the underlying data — like proving you're over 18 without showing your birthdate.
-   **Compliance twist:** Users can generate a ZKP proving their funds did *not* originate from a known illicit source (a public blocklist) — without revealing which deposit is theirs.

> "My withdrawal is one of 100 in this pool, and it is NOT from the 5 known illicit deposits."

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Privacy Pools is still experimental (co-authored by Vitalik Buterin). It represents a broader trend: cryptographic tools that provide privacy to legitimate users while *reducing* the utility of the system for illicit actors — rather than treating privacy and compliance as opposites.
:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide establishes privacy pools as an attempt to preserve privacy while excluding obviously tainted funds from the anonymity set. It matters here because privacy technology is evolving in response to both enforcement pressure and public criticism. Emphasize that newer designs try to differentiate 'privacy' from 'indiscriminate laundering support.'

**Key Points**
- Privacy pools aim to let users prove separation from known illicit deposits while still hiding exact transaction details.
- The design reflects a broader trend toward selective disclosure rather than absolute opacity.
- Define selective disclosure briefly as revealing limited compliance-relevant information without exposing everything.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@gjorgjev_blockchainforensicsunmasking_2025; @atlam_blockchainforensicssystematic_2024

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## The Shift in Strategy: Privacy-Preserving Blockchains

While CoinJoin and mixing add obfuscation *on top of* transparent ledgers, some cryptocurrencies are designed with privacy as their default, primary feature.

-   **Transparent Ledgers (Bitcoin, Ethereum):** The entire transaction graph is public. Forensics is about **analyzing** the graph.
-   **Privacy-Preserving Ledgers (Monero, Zcash):** The graph is intentionally **hidden or broken**. Forensics shifts to metadata, endpoints, and voluntary disclosures.

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide establishes the strategic shift from obfuscating on transparent ledgers to using systems designed around privacy from the start. It matters here because analysts must distinguish between privacy features bolted onto open chains and privacy-native ecosystems. Emphasize that the investigative toolkit changes dramatically when the base layer itself conceals flows.

**Key Points**
- Privacy-preserving chains reduce the usefulness of classic graph heuristics by hiding amounts, senders, or receivers at the protocol level.
- Investigations in these environments rely more heavily on endpoints and off-chain evidence.
- Define privacy-preserving blockchain briefly as a chain whose core protocol intentionally conceals transactional details from public observers.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@koe_zeromonerosecond_2020; @electriccoincompany_zcashbasicszcash_2019

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Monero (XMR): Privacy by Default

Monero hides the sender, receiver, and amount of every transaction by default via three technologies:

1.  **Ring Signatures:** Hides the **sender**. The true input is mixed with "decoy" UTXOs — an observer cannot determine which was spent.
2.  **Stealth Addresses:** Hides the **receiver**. A new one-time address is created per transaction; the recipient's public address is never recorded on-chain.
3.  **RingCT:** Hides the **amount**. Amounts are encrypted, but miners can verify no new money was created.

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide establishes Monero as the main example of privacy by default rather than privacy by optional service use. It matters here because Monero represents a fundamentally harder forensic environment than Bitcoin or Ethereum. Emphasize that sender, receiver, and amount protection are protocol-level features.

**Key Points**
- Monero combines stealth addresses, ring signatures, and confidential amounts to obscure all major transaction fields.
- Because privacy is default, investigators cannot rely on voluntary user adoption patterns the way they might in Zcash.
- Define stealth address briefly as a one-time destination address derived so outside observers cannot link it publicly to the recipient.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@koe_zeromonerosecond_2020; @monero_stealthaddress_2025; @monerocommunityundermit_moneroprivatekey_2025

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Monero: Known Forensic Weaknesses

Despite strong privacy, Monero has known investigative attack surfaces:

-   **Historical ring size failures:** Pre-2017 Monero used ring size 1 — making those transactions fully traceable. Older outputs on the chain retain this weakness.
-   **Endpoint correlation:** Monero must be bought and sold at exchanges. Correlating a XMR purchase (known amount, known time) with a subsequent sale of similar value and timing remains a viable approach — even without touching the chain.
-   **IRS bounty program:** In 2020, the IRS awarded contracts to **Chainalysis** and **CipherTrace** to develop Monero tracing capabilities — indicating the government believes partial tracing is achievable under specific conditions, though the results remain classified.

::: {style="position: relative; z-index: -1; top: -150px; max-height: 200px;"}
```{dot}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 1.8
digraph MoneroWeakness {
  graph [bgcolor="transparent"];
  rankdir=LR;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11, fillcolor="#f5f7fb"];
  edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10];

  buy [label="Buy XMR\nat Exchange\n(KYC)", fillcolor="#fdd"];
  chain [label="Monero Chain\n(opaque)", fillcolor="#e8e8e8", style="rounded,filled,dashed"];
  sell [label="Sell XMR\nat Exchange\n(KYC)", fillcolor="#fdd"];

  buy -> chain [label="entry"];
  chain -> sell [label="exit", style=dashed];
  buy -> sell [label="correlate:\namount + timing", style=dashed, color="#e74c3c", fontcolor="#e74c3c"];
}
```
:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide establishes that even Monero has practical weaknesses, though they often arise at the edges rather than in its cryptography. It matters here because students should avoid absolutist thinking about either perfect privacy or perfect tracing. Emphasize the difference between protocol strength and user or exchange weakness.

**Key Points**
- Monero's strongest weaknesses tend to appear at on-ramps, off-ramps, metadata leaks, or poor operational behavior.
- Privacy features reduce visibility but do not eliminate all correlation opportunities.
- Define endpoint leakage briefly as information exposed when a user buys, sells, stores, or operationally mishandles an otherwise private asset.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@koe_zeromonerosecond_2020; @chainalysis_reports_2025; @trmlabs_trmlabsreports_2025; @l35_ciphertrace_monero_2020
